Translating Database Errors

Two bugs found by smoke-testing this lesson's own DELETE endpoint, and the fix that closes both at once.

Manually testing DELETE /tickets/:id against a real seeded database (this lesson's ticket had a comment on it already) turned up a real bug: Prisma refused the delete — a Comment row still pointed at that ticket through a foreign key — and the raw error reached the client as a 500 with Prisma's own internal error text leaked straight into the response body. Creating a Tag with a name that already existed did the same thing for a different reason (MySQL's UNIQUE constraint on Tag.name, from Lesson 2's schema). Neither is really a 500 — both are the client asking for something the data won't allow, which is what 4xx statuses are for.

Prisma gives every one of its own "known request" errors a .code — a handful of them map cleanly onto HTTP statuses:

// Figure 3.3: recognising Prisma's own error codes (src/middleware/errorHandler.js, excerpt)
const PRISMA_ERROR_STATUS = {
  P2002: 409, // unique constraint failed (e.g. a Tag name that already exists)
  P2003: 409, // foreign key constraint failed (e.g. deleting a Ticket with Comments)
  P2025: 404, // the record a query expected to find/update/delete doesn't exist
};

const describePrismaError = (err) => {
  switch (err.code) {
    case 'P2002':
      return `A record with that ${err.meta?.target ?? 'value'} already exists`;
    case 'P2003':
      return 'This record cannot be deleted or changed because other records still depend on it';
    case 'P2025':
      return 'The requested record was not found';
    default:
      return 'Database request failed';
  }
};

409 Conflict is the right status for both cases here: the request is well-formed, but doing it would conflict with the current state of the data (a name that must be unique, or a row other rows still depend on). Neither maps to a friendlier fix like cascading the delete automatically — silently deleting a ticket's whole comment history because of one DELETE call on the ticket itself is exactly the kind of surprising behavior a support desk shouldn't have; the client has to delete the comments first, on purpose.

The handler itself decides when to reach for this map, and — just as important — never lets an error it doesn't recognise leak its raw message either:

// Figure 3.4: deciding the status, and hiding the internals of a real 500 (src/middleware/errorHandler.js, excerpt)
export default (err, req, res, next) => {
  let status = err.status;
  let message = err.message;

  if (!status && err instanceof Prisma.PrismaClientKnownRequestError && PRISMA_ERROR_STATUS[err.code]) {
    status = PRISMA_ERROR_STATUS[err.code];
    message = describePrismaError(err);
  }

  status = status || 500;

  if (status === 500) {
    console.error(err);
    message = 'Internal Server Error';
  }

  res.status(status).json({ error: { message } });
};

err.status still wins first — an ApiError a controller threw on purpose (previous slide) already knows exactly what it wants to say. Only when nothing set a status and the error is specifically a Prisma.PrismaClientKnownRequestError with a code this project recognises does the Prisma-specific message take over. Anything left over — a genuine bug, not a client mistake — falls through to 500, gets logged with console.error so it's still visible in the terminal, but the client only ever sees the generic 'Internal Server Error': the raw message might describe a file path, a SQL fragment, or other internals that have no business leaving this server.
